Inside Retro Reset, the "really inspirational" father and son project teaching kids about classic games hardware from aboard a converted bus

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At first the kids jostle to get to the games that they know.
  • Recent findings suggest that luke’s knowledge is beautiful but the students also find him approachable.
  • The bleeps and blips start from the machines as the students start playing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At first the kids jostle to get to the games that they know. "Welcome to the Retro Reset Bus," notes Luke Stoner as the students push to get to the screen that’s caught their eye. Sonic on the Sega Mega Drive is the first they see, and the quickest student to get on board the bus looks triumphant as he nabs the stool in front of the console. Jason, Luke’s dad, asks him what he thinks about the graphics – slightly grainy and slightly pixelated – but he’s not at all bothered and soon engrossed. After a few minutes, though, his eyes keep moving to the back of the bus where "Jackson is a wally" is now emblazoned across a flickering screen in seven different colours. Jackson then gives out a chuffed yell when his code finally works after a couple of restarts. His retort to his mate appears on the 1981 BBC Micro Model B‘s screen as the other students crane to have a look. This is, incidentally, the machine that turned a national broadcaster into a computer retailer (with help from Acorn), says Jason.

Recent findings suggest that luke’s knowledge is beautiful but the students also find him approachable. As Jason shares: "It’s really inspirational for kids coming onto a bus that they can talk to someone younger like Luke, who knows his stuff and has made something incredible happen." One student asks where Minecraft is and Luke explains that it doesn’t fit the parameter of being more than twenty years old yet, sharing details of when it was published and by who. Roblox could be included, but Luke isn’t keen because of recent controversies around safety. When this group are reluctantly herded off the bus by even more reluctant teachers, another heads in with just a little gap for resetting the machines and cramming a biscuit.

The bleeps and blips start from the machines as the students start playing. One teacher stops at the Atari 2600 and shares that her family has just bought her one. She is loving the daily dose of nostalgia. Luke and Jason move up and down the bus answering questions, resetting machines and showing the students their collection of old phones. One student winces at he is passed the bag that would have carried the battery for a Panasonic EB-3600 "brick" phone from 1989. When Jason indicates his dad had one, they give that look of pity reserved for anyone over 30 but are also incredulous that anyone would lug that around, especially when the phone could only do calls. When Jason asks if anyone would like to break an iPhone and have a look inside, all of the hands shoot up. He then talks about memory, RAM and chips, brings out a floppy disk; and tells the tale of where the expression "computer bug" came from. Still, it's the game on a tape - Jungle Story for the Commodore 64 - which they all turn away from screens to see. Perhaps we have Stranger Things to thank, but the tape has retro currency and they all think it’s sick.

The event is being run by East Sussex Careers Hub and is specifically aimed at students with SEND (Special Educational Needs and Disabilities). More than twenty-five schools turn up and most teachers leave with a flyer, chatting to colleagues about where the bus could park onsite. Jason indicates that the response to the bus, since Retro Reset's launch as a registered charity in August 2025, has been phenomenal, and they could easily fill a full week with visits. For now, he is juggling it with work commitments.

The bus was Luke’s idea and inspired by a visit to The Centre for Computing History in Cambridge, where visitors can get their hands on home computers and consoles from decades gone by. The family started thinking about what was possible and finally, after Luke finished college, began kitting out the bus: buying or accepting donations of hardware, researching which monitors would work with the ancient systems, and installing it all within the cabin.

It has been revealed that on a basic level, the charity is telling the story of how technology has iterated. But by allowing visitors to take apart their machines, and giving brief lessons in coding with Basic, it also pulls the veil back on the work that goes into making a game - while opening students' eyes to what they could create themselves. "I guess it’s bridging the gap between the polished and finished latest game," Jason notes, "which could be perceived as not achievable for them, to seeing how all that coding came about. Other than making sure they are really accurate with their typing; they realise that coding can be quite simple and something that they can actually do. I would go further and say that when they have written some code, nearly all of them have a significant smile on their face." This, he hopes, might be the spark for some students to get into coding, especially for PC games, where under-18s are an underrepresented demographic.

According to recent reports, it also hit the road as the popularity of retro gaming continued to surge. According to a Consumer Reports survey published last February, 14% of US gamers regularly play games made before 2000. This is reflected in the staggering stat that the retro gaming market is estimated to be worth $3.8 billion globally, with a projected rise to $8 billion by 2033. Retro-focused videos on YouTube and TikTok rack up millions of views of views, and communities formed on reddit or Discord - some with hundreds of thousands of members - discuss nothing else.

In a recent development, nostalgia is playing a huge part. Atari’s Implicit Conversations is built on just this, creating retro games for modern consoles like PlayStation 5 or the Nintendo Switch. For Luke, though, this misses the point. He likes the click when you put a cartridge in a machine; and he likes that he is just him and the game. The parents of visiting students appreciate this too, and often share how overwhelming it feels to keep their kids safe in the online gaming environment. "Parents of younger children [tell us that] they hate that Minecraft and Roblox can allow their kids to play against perceived strangers. Even the more technical parents say they still miss safety measures and would prefer the games not be online at all," Jason explains.

Last month, Ofcom published its Growing Up Gaming summary report, which found that almost two-thirds (64%) of parents of three to 17 year olds who game online are concerned about their child talking to strangers through games or their chat functions. And, while the vast majority of young players go online without incident, it is true that those who use chat functions will likely interact with strangers. The same research found that more than half (55%) of children who game online say they play with people they have never met offline at least sometimes, while one in five (20%) do so all or most of the time they play.

According to recent reports, by contrast, Jason claims that not one student has asked if they can get online, and he’s also never seen one get out their phone when they’re on the bus. Perhaps it is a welcomed break. "We offer a completely safe environment to come and experience these games and machines. That's really what we're here for," he states.

Luke shares too that he became nervous of the data he was sharing with gaming companies, and conscious that this was all being stored, thus making it vulnerable to breaches. He also baulked at what he felt was a constant money grab from gaming companies, including moves that render games unsupported or completely obsolete. Retro gaming is cheap in comparison and therefore more accessible, especially for younger players. "When you tell them that they can get an old console for less than £100 and often games come free when you buy them second hand, their ears really prick up," Jason says. "For a lot of the youngsters, the cost of modern gaming equipment is unattainable. And of course, we explain that they could take old computers and laptops and then load free operating software onto them. This gets them online, often for free. Once they are there, they can game.".

John W. Champeau is founder of Champ Games, a Connecticut-based venture, which develops retro games system primarily for the Atari 2600. He has Scramble, Galagon, Gorf Arcade and Elevator Agent on his line-up. He agrees that price point is a huge part of the appeal of retro gaming. "Atari has released a line of "+" systems that are modern reinterpretations of the class Atari 2600 and 7800 hardware, but at a lower price point but with modern conveniences such as HDMI support, firmware updates, and new controllers," he notes. These systems can also play older cartridges that were released back in the day. "This means that the games themselves can be acquired at a low cost as well, sometimes even free if someone is lucky enough to know someone with a box of old Atari carts in their basement or attic.".

Industry observers note that but there may also be something intrinsically different about how these games are designed to be played that is driving their renaissance. In December 2025, Newsweek shared the views of two mental health professionals that "90s Video Games Were Better for Kids’ Brains." In what was sure to be a contentious piece (and perhaps that was the point), mental health counsellor Veronica Lichtenstein, and Melissa Gallagher, a licensed clinical social worker, argued that the very nature of gaming has changed and is now damaging. Retro games had a start and an end – and with the latter came a massive hit of dopamine for achieving victory. Modern games are designed as "loops for addiction" with no real end; and constant prompts to buy. Satisfaction is constantly deferred. Lichtenstein also says that modern games leave little room for critical thinking, as a quick search online will delivers solutions if a player ever gets stuck.

Champeau agrees. "Our games are not designed to be addictive 'time stealers' like some modern video games that encourage players to 'stay online' for hours on end to acquire additional resources needed to complete a game or advance to a upcoming level, etc," he says, adding: "All of our games are designed to be short burst distractions that don't rely on long gaming sessions to feel a sense of accomplishment.” He says that the lower graphics resolution and primitive sounds are actually a relief for many after years of hyper-realistic gaming. "Retro games distance the gap between game and reality, which was the intention of video games in the first place," he argues.

Recent findings suggest that back on the bus, Sonic may have attracted the initial crowds but it is now Pacman and the Binatone that the students are huddling around. Jason has given up one control for the tennis game to a student and a noisy competition is now taking place. The graphics are basic as is the premise, but scoring is tricky and the battle to get to 15 points hard-fought. The teacher laughs. "The bleeps from that game are bringing back memories," she claims as she tries to encourage her students to finish and hand over the controllers. But with faces lit up by the screen and set in concentration, they don’t hear her. This is play for play’s sake, with no distractions, and could be why the games of the past might be just the future these kids need.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you've noticed that Grand Theft Auto 6's Jason Duval isn't much of a talker, that's by design, as his quiet nature was inspired by Steve McQueen and the studio's research into former Army Rangers.

Speaking to Destructoid over email, Rockstar's senior vice president of narrative, Rupert Humphries, explained that the team looked at classic couple-on-the-run films when it decided on GTA 6's story.

Sources indicate that "When we decided we wanted to tell a story about a couple on the run, we looked at all the similar kinds of movies, and one of the ones that really stood out was Peckinpah's The Getaway," Humphries said. "Steve McQueen was famous for pulling lines out of scripts and saying things with his presence alone. We wanted to see how close we could get to that with a game character, where so many of our protagonists have been the opposite.".

That approach also fitted the studio's research into veterans. "This also resonated with the research we were doing around veterans and particularly former Army Rangers (in our world we call them Marauders)," Humphries continued. "These guys typically aren't running their mouths or reacting to something unless it's strictly necessary, while still being strong and still asserting themselves.".

Game writer Michael Wiafe stated Florida's real-life crime stories were "an obvious starting point" for GTA 6's characters more broadly.

According to recent reports, "From then on, it was about coming up with authentic characters that didn't stray too far from reality but also were not totally bound by it either," Wiafe said. "The majority of our main characters are undeniably reprehensible on paper, full-blown criminals, but also decent human beings. Their moral makeup isn't necessarily cut-and-dry, and we don't attempt to make excuses for them.".

Industry observers note that fellow writer Elizabeth Gauvey-Kern added that while "the story takes some pretty heavy turns", Jason and Lucia's goal remains consistent. "So sharing their sense of determination, the focus on their goal, through all the highs and lows - that's what I hope people feel more than anything. You really want them to make it.".

GTA 6 launched on Thursday, 19th November, for PS5 and Xbox Series X/S, and while it's the biggest entertainment launch of all time, selling 32.5 million pre-release copies and making $3.79 billion by the end of its first day, not everyone is happy: some players have been review bombing its Metacritic user score over its limited FPS and purported "woke" agenda.

Industry observers note that eurogamer called GTA 6 an open world of "awe, minute detail and impossible scale" in our five-star GTA 6 review. If you need help getting through the game now that it's here, you can check out Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough and a breakdown of our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

Just don't share any, uh, spicy in-game screenshots via PSN - we recently learned that a GTA 6 player was hit with a 30-day PlayStation Network ban after sending a friend a photo they took in the game's nudist resort.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Anyway, I’m writing about playing GTA 6 on console because it’s led me to conclude that a particular aspect of GTA 5’s PC port - one I’ve always rather taken for granted - could be a bigger deal for the inevitable Windows version of 6 than even the usual go-to PC plus points.
  • As Rockstar’s offerings have shuffled away from arcadey rampage facilitators and ever deeper into the mould of uber-detailed life of crime sims, however, they've also began letting players see things directly through the eyes of the crim whose blood-splattered shoes they’ve stepped into.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been playing GTA 6 on PS5.

To be fair, I’ve made no secret of my plans to do just that if you’ve read any of our recent roundups of what everyone’s playing over the weekend. I can understand why it might leave a sour taste in the mouth, but it is what it is. No corporate gun has been pointed at my head as a mandate to temporarily forsake my PC and play the big game of the moment is forced into my hands.

Anyway, I’m writing about playing GTA 6 on console because it’s led me to conclude that a particular aspect of GTA 5’s PC port - one I’ve always rather taken for granted - could be a bigger deal for the inevitable Windows version of 6 than even the usual go-to PC plus points. You know, better graphics, superior performance, and modding. Historically, Rockstar’s crime sandboxes are games played from the third person perspective. That shot lingering behind Niko Bellic as he jogs around Brooklyn with a rocket launcher or following the damn bike of CJ as he in turn follows that damn train. This is the default way GTA’s breakneck action is presented to the player and was with GTA 5 at launch.

As Rockstar’s offerings have shuffled away from arcadey rampage facilitators and ever deeper into the mould of uber-detailed life of crime sims, however, they've also began letting players see things directly through the eyes of the crim whose blood-splattered shoes they’ve stepped into. In order to do that, while simultaneously pushing the detail and graphical boundaries of their rendered worlds, Rockstar have needed to squeeze every bit of juice they can from the available hardware. Red Dead Redemption 2 managed to include a full first person mode at launch. GTA 6 hasn’t been so lucky, even if there are moments when bringing up your phone or reading a note temporarily lodges the camera into Jason and Lucia’s noggins.

There is a way to glitch yourself into a more permanent first person perspective, but it’s naturally not got the polish that a proper first person mode would. What it does do is make clear that, with vehicle interiors lavishly detailed and some gun animations looking natural rather than janky, any port using the PC's extra horses to deliver a proper first person mode seems a no brainer, if not something already set in stone.

Assuming that is the case, I frankly can’t see why first person won’t become the go-to perspective on PC. Even more so than RDR2, GTA 6 feels like a game built to belong in first person. It dedicates so much time and energy to engaging you in every aspect of Jason and Lucia’s routines, rendering everything from eating to working out to doing up a house (and the acts involved in doing a robbery, I guess) in such exhaustive detail and depth that it’s almost beyond parody.

It has been revealed that notifications ping about you needing to finish a bench pressing session where every rep involves holding and releasing R2 and L2 at just the right time. An app tells you you’re hungry, so you wander over to the fridge, pick out a protein shake to down, then press R2 to lob the bottle in the bin, assuming you’re keen to keep your flat tidy. Shopping trips see you pick up groceries off shelves, stow them in a bag, then run home with it tucked under your arm because you’ve brought a motorbike and forgotten it lacks a boot. Every stickup begins with the ritual of picking your longarm gun out of your car’s boot, where it might have sat next to a bag of drugs you’ve stowed to deliver to a fence later. Stopping off to switch cars and clothes to throw the cops off your scent is no longer just for overenthusiastic roleplayers.

The fact that the game goes to such lengths only to maintain the detachment inherent to the third person view feels bizarrely antithetical at times, like an exhibition of a tiny Fabergé egg that you’re forced to view through a telescope from the surface of Mars. The massive efforts of Rockstar’s developers - many of whom are right now trying to gain formal union recognition or have been fighting the tech giant at an employment tribunal over firings they argue were unjust - went into putting together an artwork that regularly ends up at an arm’s length out of necessity, despite packing intricacies likely best seen through a magnifying glass.

Enter the PC release. And possibly nothing else offering the same bang for your buck around the same time. With GTA 5, the PS4 and Xbox One got an enhanced version of the game around the time of the PC port, offering a number of extra features - including a first person mode. Rockstar were quick to rule out GTA 6 getting 60 or 40fps performance modes on current console hardware due to a lack of horses, and if that also applies to a first person mode, then such a thing might only come with the next generation of consoles. That’d be the PS6 and Xbox’s Project Helix, neither of which seem hugely imminent and could well end up boasting ludicrous prices thanks to the ongoing memory shortages.

Sources indicate that so, those who already own a PC capable of running any GTA 6 port could be in the best position to enjoy the game from a Jason and Lucia-eye view the moment such a thing becomes possible. Sure, it would also look and run better, but to be brutally honest I’ve found it looks damn gorgeous and runs acceptably on PS5. Sure, modding will no doubt spring up must-have additions, but the base game already works in plenty of the roleplaying mechanics and in-depth side-jobbing that a lot of popular GTA 5 mods delivered.

According to recent reports, thus, that window as the place to play GTA 6 as it feels intended, in first person, is what I’d currently peg as the best chance for the crimsim to be not just a great game you can play on PC - as I’d argue Red Dead Redemption 2 and GTA 5 are - but a great PC game that’s inarguably best experienced on our platform of choice. I don’t think writing that is falling into the trap it’s easy to end up in with major games that hit console first: declaring in salesman-like fashion that they’ll of course be better on PC by default, in a manner that sometimes feels a bit like you’re trying to convince yourself that you’ve not paid more than a pre-RAM crisis console buyer for nothing.

I’d never consider playing Cyberpunk 2077 in anything but first person on PC. GTA 6, from what I’ve played thus far, could be the next uber-detailed open world I spend hundreds of hours taking in the sights of, ideally through the eyes of a highly dangerous and highly stylish operator on the prowl for lucrative underworld opportunities.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, call of Duty publisher Activision has filed for a upcoming patent allowing it to train NPCs on real-world player voice chat.
  • Industry observers note that the patent, spotted by Patentlyze, was filed in July and published in November.
  • The system compares those captured player reactions and then correlates them with coinciding gameplay events in order to understand their significance, essentially learning as it goes what triggers certain reactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, call of Duty publisher Activision has filed for a upcoming patent allowing it to train NPCs on real-world player voice chat. The patent describes an AI-driven system that listens in on player voice chat following key gameplay moments and later recreates it using in-game characters.

Industry observers note that the patent, spotted by Patentlyze, was filed in July and published in November. According to the filing and its diagrams, the system is a self-learning neural network that recognises major gameplay moments - such as kills, longshots, deaths and so on - and records the player's reaction and voice chat from the moment just before and then after they happen. These can be as simple as brief celebratory shouts, groans or yells, or as complex as trash talk.

The system compares those captured player reactions and then correlates them with coinciding gameplay events in order to understand their significance, essentially learning as it goes what triggers certain reactions. The AI then teaches itself to promptly identify those when they occur in-game and replicate them.

In a recent development, although the replicated voice lines don't directly repeat players' own chat, the system does keep a profile of each player it analyses so it can deliver a response tailored to them, including sticking to the same spoken language, which it uses large language models (LLMs) to help identify. The patent describes a filter of sorts to keep NPCs from learning offensive language such as slurs.

According to the patent, the system's reach extends beyond in-game voice chat to also potentially access voice comms from major apps like Discord.

Activision's goal is to create NPCs that can speak naturally, rather than re-use the same pre-recorded lines. The application seems to be limited to multiplayer games, including those with co-op. Think of the generic voice lines spoken by AI-teammates like "cover me" and so on in a PvE game, or the many other similar ones in battle royale and PvP matches that contain dozens or hundreds of players.

Incidentally, the patent talks of replacing those generic messages with learned ones for players who join a match without a microphone, but players can also seemingly allow their in-game avatars to always use generated voices.

As the game industry continues to grapple with the use of generative-AI in game development, Activision's patent seems to be going directly to source, recreating how those LLMs and AI systems got their knowledge to begin with: from humans.

It has been revealed that if you've been a fan of Grand Theft Auto for a while, you might have noticed a strange absence in GTA 6. While the game is packed full of different activities, the recurring pastime of darts is missing, having been present in GTA 5, GTA Online, and GTA 4.

The reason for the lack of darts in Grand Theft Auto 6? Well, according to Rockstar North co-studio lead Rob Nelson, it's a simple case of Rockstar having too little time and resources to make it to a high standard.

It has been revealed that nelson told VGC: "The darts one is a contentious one. Even we... You hear they have unlimited money or unlimited time, even we do not and so sometimes you just have to admit we are not going to be able to make this to the level we feel we need to.".

Nelson elaborated that since Red Dead Redemption 2, Rockstar has taken to expanding what were small mini-games into full-on activities. He pointed to basketball in GTA 6 as an example, which you can play in a way that feels like an extension of gameplay with "fluid" movement. Even if it's a relatively small chunk of the game, a lot of time went into making it feel like "a game in its own right", Nelson said. And the same is true of pool.

"A lot of work [is needed] to get it tuned right. Darts is one we just didn't get to," Nelson said. The studio "didn't have the resources" to include it in the game and have it up to par. "It's better not to do it than to do it and have it not be good enough," he said.

Even without darts, there are plenty of side activities in Grand Theft Auto 6 that help expand Vice City. This includes diving and treasure hunting and fishing, both of which you unlock near the start of the game. If you're looking for a guide of all there is to do in the game, Eurogamer's GTA 6 walkthrough is a good place to start. We've also got a breakdown of all the GTA 6 cheats if you needed an extra hand getting through the game.

Sources indicate that if you take a look at Metacritics' best games of all time list, you'll see Grand Theft Auto 6 sitting pretty at the top spot. Yet, if you take a gander at some of the others following close behind it, you may notice a sudden increase in very negative reviews from those riding hard for Rockstar's latest release.

Take the user reviews for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which held the top spot for years prior to GTA 6's launch. You can see such pearls of wisdom as: "L Japanese Propaganda. Industry observers note that the same is true for the original Soul Calibur. Its user reviews includes newly delivered pieces of critique like this from user GTABEST2456: "Slop game dethroned by GTA 6, 99 on metacritic N1, now this is third LOOOOOOL, get rekt. I played through and I wish there was less zelda references more niko bellic.".

Even Super Mario Galaxy 2 wasn't safe. Users have taken to review- bombing this game too, an example being BoroqueTsunami who wrote: "Peak Nintendoslop ️ Jump man gimmick. Y'all thought it was sweet until Rockstar pulled up." All of these reviews, across all these non-GTA 6 games, were written following the release of Grand Theft Auto 6.

While it is unclear whether GTA 6 fans shot the first bullet here, or whether anti-GTA 6 Metacritic brigaders are to blame, what is apparent is GTA 6 is itself being hit with a counter-offensive of sorts. "Retaliation for Zelda review bombing," wrote user Lucius26. "I didn't choose this war, but I'll fight it all the same. GTA fans, we were not your enemy. GTA6 just made people mad. You like a bad game, accept that.".

It has been revealed that this is all obviously silly and only helps to make the user review section of Metacritic less helpful for people actually trying to get a gist of what these games are like from members of the public. This also stems from a lack of verification on whether people have actually played these games before writing their takes.

Whether events like this will prompt Metacritic to implement some additional quality control remains to be seen, though it has been a continuous problem for a while now and this is hardly the first time review-bombing has been used by some of the more bizarre fans of big-budget releases. In fairness, Metacritic is not the only platform to have suffered from this. Steam, too, has had a history of user review-bombing, with Valve adding features to help curb this over the years.

As reported by VGC, Darren Evenson — who was a senior game designer at New Radical Games, the team thought to be producing the Hit & Run revival — has posted on LinkedIn about projects being cancelled at the studio.

"It seems that not even a fantastic project with an absolutely incredible team is immune from the current state of the industry right now, as what we were working on at Newly introduced Radical Games (although mind-blowingly awesome) was part of a whole gaggle of cancellations," Evenson states.

Recent findings suggest that "Oh, you silly suits with spreadsheets... will you EVER learn? If you don't make the game, you can't make the money... and if you don't make the money, then you don't get the power... and... well, there's more to that quote, but I digress.

For the first time in my career, I am Available For Work and looking for a new exciting opportunity where I can make some fun games with some great people!

Please reach out, shout out, or peform some interpretive dance if you know of an opportunity that a hip cat like me could groove to.".

Fans who have spotted this message are fairly confident, based on certain quotes, that it's referring to The Simpsons: Hit & Run, though others have suggested it could actually be Scarface: The World Is Yours.

Fresh Radical Games is a recently founded studio with many key staff from Radical Entertainment, the Canadian outfit that made the original Hit & Run.

Between that and the show's creator, Matt Groening, practically confirming the remake's existence, it was thought that it was finally going to happen.

While this newly introduced message doesn't outright say the remake is cancelled, something has been, and Hit & Run was the most obvious candidate for the studio's main project.

We'll have to wait and see how things play out, but for now, it feels like the elusive remake may not be so close as we thought, and may in fact not be coming at all.

Industry observers note that what do you think? Tell us in the comments section below.

[source videogameschronicle.com].

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (385 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Eurogamer

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto 6 runs at 30 frames-per-second across all the consoles it's at the moment available on, including the more powerful PlayStation 5 Pro.
  • Reddit user Meowwie64 devised a way to essentially unlock GTA 6's frame-rate on Series X.
  • Recent findings suggest that in a detailed post, Meowwie64 shared the steps they used to trigger their glitch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6 runs at 30 frames-per-second across all the consoles it's at the moment available on, including the more powerful PlayStation 5 Pro. The game doesn't offer a 60fps performance mode or an option to unlock the frame-rate, but one industrious player has managed to do it anyway on Xbox.

Reddit user Meowwie64 devised a way to essentially unlock GTA 6's frame-rate on Series X. Their hack relied on the Xbox's rarely-discussed Quick Resume feature, which lets you park multiple games in memory and switch between them without having to re-load each game.

Recent findings suggest that in a detailed post, Meowwie64 shared the steps they used to trigger their glitch. For starters, you're going to need a 120Hz monitor display or TV, as the glitch requires adjusting refresh rates.

Industry observers note that first, you need to limit Xbox to display at 60Hz under the console Settings menu. Then, you start GTA 6 (version 01.002.001), wait until the six-star logo appears and then go back to Xbox Settings to change the refresh rate to 120Hz.

Sources indicate that before you return to GTA 6, the final step requires launching another game on your console. This has to be a cold boot, meaning the game shouldn't already be running parked in Quick Resume.

After the second game launches, you now need to use Quick Resume to resume playing GTA 6, which is when you're going to notice the higher frame-rate. The Reddit user noted the game could reach 90-plus FPS at certain moments.

Unfortunately, the user also discovered that game-speed appears to be tied to frame-rate in GTA 6, at least when it comes to certain gameplay animations and when performing certain actions. "I have a stable 90fps and everything works fine but Jason's animations run at 2x speed or more," Meowwie64 wrote. Incidentally, cutscenes do not appear to be affected by this problem, so they run at their normal speed.

As much as a 30fps frame-rate makes GTA 6 feel less smooth and potentially less enjoyable to play compared to 60fps or higher, none of the current-generation consoles are capable of delivering frame-rates beyond that. Tech experts Digital Foundry recently explained why even the PS5 Pro isn't powerful enough to run the game at 60fps or even 40fps.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gaming tech giant Nvidia has decided to reinstate Jensen Huang as its president and CEO, despite allegedly saying it wouldn't, and despite a string of extramarital affairs and investigations into alleged bullying, workplace harassment, and humiliation.

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia's Chair Harvey C. Jones declared on behalf of the Nvidia's board today - the same person reported as saying the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO".

"We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Tech giant. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as Nvidia's chief financial officer.".

In the same press release, Huang said he was "honoured" to return to the manufacturer "at the beginning of a newly introduced industrial revolution". "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," Huang said.

However, the investigation into one of Huang's extramarital affairs - the one with the person US intelligence believes to be a Chinese spy - will "proceed to conclusion". The manufacturer also mentioned it formed a "National Security and Export Control Committee", with independent directors, in relation to this.

Huang resigned on 12th November a few days after his affair with the alleged Chinese spy came to light. Two subsequent affairs - both said to be with Nvidia employees and therefore his subordinates - were unearthed not long after, putting increased pressure on Huang and Nvidia.

Since his departure, Nvidia stock has tanked, and as news of his reinstatement spreads around the world, it has sharply recovered again.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that enhancement, 26th Nov: Yesterday I posted a version of this article in which I, and other RPS staff, got a number of things badly, badly wrong. The purpose of this update is not to hide from the consequences but to limit the harm inflicted by a specific section of the original text, which has been replaced in the highlighted section below.

Industry observers note that I'm both furious at myself and intensely sorry to everyone hurt by the original version. We've published a followup post here.

Hello and welcome to an unusually not-Supporter exclusive ed letter, its paywall laying unbuilt so we can exchange some Real Talk with as many RPS readers as possible.

Recent findings suggest that S'been a weird one, hasn't it? The biggest game release of a generation, a bonafide cultural event that's touched everything from the highest reaches of government to B&Q adverts, and yet Grand Theft Auto VI's lack of a PC version has kind of given it the feeling of a well-budgeted fireworks display going off outside your bedroom window. For me, anyway.

It has been revealed that the question of how to cover GTA 6 editorially is one we've spent months back-and-forthing over in meetings. Even if you consider "It's too big to ignore" a cop-out argument, the likelihood of it eventually coming to PC - based on historical precedent - is practically certain, making it at least partially fair game. At the same time, no, it is not 'a PC game' in its current form, and enthusiastically plastering the front page with coverage of something most of our readers probably can't play – with, say, a launch day liveblog, or a 100-hour-review-that-isn't-a-review-honest – would just be mad.

Recent findings suggest that I'm quite happy with what we ended up with: continued but not excessive coverage of developments around the game, ongoing reporting on Rockstar's labour issues, and several consecutive days of irreverent posting about the other open-world crime games you can (or shouldn't) play. Why, then, was this restrained approach on the editorial side paired with near-blanket GTA output from our guides team?

The answer to that is the same answer we've been giving to anyone who's asked why RPS previously went as hard as we did on Baldur's Gate 3 or Starfield or Elden Ring: site's gotta eat. It is almost impossible to overstate how important guides are to the survival of a mostly-free games website, or frankly, how much better Ollie, Jeremy, Callum, Dion, and all our guiding 'lancers are at keeping the lights on than the rest of us. An example, which hopefully won't get me in trouble with the higher-ups for sharing 'business intelligence,' is that my piece on Derelikt - one of the most conventionally RPS-y features we ran during GTA 6 launch week - attracted nought point five percent of the eyeballs as Guides Gang's list of GTA strip clubs.

Some sites would look at that and think, well, guess we ought to stop writing about scratchy indie games and focus entirely on megablockbusters. We never have. Our way might create a bit of a parallel reality, where a section of the site does treat GTA 6 like a live PC game, but when those guides effectively fund, support, or otherwise enable the more diverse and offbeat editorial operation, you can't convince me it isn't the best way that's currently feasible.

Industry observers note that somewhere we can do better, however, is how we cover AI - genAI in particular. To start with, I'll temporarily yield the ed letter writing yoke back to Julian, who's on holiday but did send me this for inclusion:.

Note: This section has been rewritten, as publishing the original text was a terrible judgement error. We apologise for making it.

It has been revealed that we've recently seen an ugly blow up in the comments under a series of articles on RPS, mostly relating to AI. While we broadly expect both writers and readers to take responsibility for the tenor of their comments, there have been multiple instances where we've either failed to create the conditions needed for civil discourse, or have allowed them to deteriorate. We need to be better on this, are sorry that we haven't been, and are particularly sorry to those individuals who we've hurt as a result.

In a recent development, I'd add, in response to suggestions I've seen that RPS could enact a side-wide policy or charter on how we discuss AI, that directives like this tend to be non-starters. Fundamental to RPS is the idea that whoever comes and goes, everyone who writes for the site has the freedom to use their own voice, to express their own opinions. This obviously doesn't extend to getting involved in Internet slapfights or personal insults, and as Edwin has noted under a recent AI-tinged story, a consequence is that our output doesn't always follow a consistent editorial stance. Still, I feel that's a price worth paying for maintaining something that, to my eyes, has always made RPS special - if sometimes a little chaotic. And, despite our recent need of the ban button, the vast majority of our readers are smart and mature enough to grasp that different writers might have different views and interpretations.

Sources indicate that for example, I don't think I'm as open as Julian to the use of genAI in games development, to be totally honest. Machine learning can and has done cool, unproblematic things for games-related tech and hardware, as well as more 'serious' business like medical imaging. But I'm yet to see anything out of contemporary genAI that outweighs its combined problems with environmental impact, poor output quality, unauthorised scraping of creative and technical works, its applications in producing misleading A/V material, and even the physical safety of impressionable chatbot users. To say nothing of the fact that Google's embrace of genAI search results presents an existential threat to sites like RPS, regardless of how many guides to finding Skunk Ape (???) we produce.

All that said, I do agree that we - all of us, fans and haters alike - would benefit from chilling out, and trying to navigate the concern with a little more thoughtfulness and a little less dunking. In keeping with the aforementioned editorial freedom, I can see myself writing less about genAI, not more, though on the occasions it does come up, I will try to articulate my opposition to it more deliberately.

Recent findings suggest that I'm also profoundly disinterested in anointing myself AI Cop, rushing to banish every confessed Claude user to the stockades; I don't have to make excuses for (or give my Advent Calendar votes to) games that adopted genAI, but if it's a matter of choosing targets, there are bigger fish to fry than individual indie games. As far as the comments go, we still only want to police actual bad behaviour, not any particular AI viewpoint, so hopefully we can join each other in this temperature-cooling and remember that "Be excellent to each other" isn't just an Eighties film reference.

To end on a jollier note, thanks to everyone who followed along with the RPS 100, another Not GTA highlight of the past week (and, indeed, 2026). I reckon this was one of the best, most vibrant lists we've done in years, owing in no small parts to the contributions of Sin, Oisin, and Jeremy P. You can vote right now for the RPS 100 Reader Edition, and our insatiable lust for ranking games will also manifest in the imminent 2026 RPS Advent Calendar, for which the reader-run Guessing Game is already open - with free RPS Supporter subscriptions as prizes. Which you might need, as future ed letters will be back as Supporter exclusives. Look, we're not made of nudity explainers.

Rockstar just issued a new patch for GTA 6 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, targeting a few challenges players have been reporting since the game debuted last Thursday (19th November).

It has been revealed that the 23rd November patch for the game deploys seven major fixes for the game, including a pretty significant bug that prevented phone calls not triggering at certain points, resulting in a scenario where you could be locked out of progressing the game. The official update is titled 'version 01.002.002', and its weighs in at different sizes on different consoles: it's 603.8 MB on PS5, and 1.6 GB on Xbox Series X/S.

Thanks to an upgrade on the Rockstar website, you can read all of the updates that arrive with the latest pathc below.

There have been a few fairly high-profile cases of the autosave not working as the developer intended, leading to a few cases of streamers losing plenty of real-world time thanks to unpredictable auto-save behaviour. JasonTheWeen lost 12 hours of progress on the PS5, for example.

But there's one issue here the developer hasn't addressed: vignetting. Plenty of players have taken to online communities to complain about the vignette effect that pops into the game - theoretically to help with motion smoothing and various grapihcal elements as the game runs in 30FPS. THe effect is worsened when you're fatigued, hungry, or have some other status effect, but it is present quite a lot of the time, too. Most of the responses to a tweet about the patch posted by the Rockstar Support account reference the vignetting in GTA 6, and the developer has issued no response at the time of writing.

Since then he was the main antagonist of Boltgun 2, and was central in the 2025 novel Achmagos.

Sources indicate that what this means for Dawn of War 4 is that, if he is a commander of Chaos forces, expect a lot of machinery and demon engines on his side. That's kind of his whole deal. Whether that means he's paired with tech-focused Dark Mechanicum as a sort of mirror to the Adeptus Mechanicus faction already in the game, or if he'll come alongside Chaos Space Marines to better reflect the Dark Angels / Blood Ravens remains to be seen. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that EA wanted a World of Warcraft killer when it bought BioWare in 2007, according to Dragon Age producer Mark Darrah.
  • It has been revealed that bioWare was first acquired in 2005 by a private equity fund alongside Pandemic Studios, makers of the original Star Wars: Battlefront games, and packaged under a single holding company.
  • In an interview for podcast Pembridge TV, Darrah explains that BioWare intentionally "made games that were bigger than other people's games," and the studio continued to expand its scope by hiring more people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that EA wanted a World of Warcraft killer when it bought BioWare in 2007, according to Dragon Age producer Mark Darrah. But he indicates BioWare's MMO, Star Wars: The Old Republic, never did WoW numbers, and EA's higher-ups always "hated" it as a result.

It has been revealed that bioWare was first acquired in 2005 by a private equity fund alongside Pandemic Studios, makers of the original Star Wars: Battlefront games, and packaged under a single holding company. While Darrah notes that he was a programmer in this era, and thus didn't have a great insight into BioWare's financial situation, his "understanding is that we basically had no money left. We needed money to continue to exist.".

In an interview for podcast Pembridge TV, Darrah explains that BioWare intentionally "made games that were bigger than other people's games," and the studio continued to expand its scope by hiring more people. While the original studio, based in Edmonton, continued to develop single-player RPGs, BioWare opened a new studio in Austin, Texas to work on the massively multiplayer online game that would become Star Wars: The Old Republic. That, Darrah believes, is the true reason EA acquired BioWare.

According to recent reports, "EA's always wanted everything to be a live service," Darrah says. "They just didn't use that language in the past. Back in the days before Destiny, the thing that was seen as the successful live service model was the MMO. Everyone wanted an MMO. World of Warcraft came out and totally redefined the space. Everyone wanted a World of Warcraft killer. I mean, it was Star Wars. Surely it could be the World of Warcraft killer.".

Sources indicate that so, as part of a package deal with BioWare's single-player RPG studio in Edmonton and Pandemic, EA bought its potential WoW killer. Darrah recalls speculating on why EA was laying out so much money for the acquisition: "It's like, 'okay, well, they really want Star Wars: The Old Republic. They want the MMO. They obviously want [Battlefront].' Then it's like, 'oh, and they're getting BioWare Edmonton.' For me, and for many people in Edmonton at the time of the acquisition, it looked like EA was buying Star Wars: The Old Republic and Pandemic and getting BioWare Edmonton as a side effect.".

Of course, Pandemic ended up being an early casualty of the acquisition, as EA shut it down in 2009. "Star Wars: The Old Republic more than paid for itself eventually, but it took a really long time. The probably single best return on investment that EA got was BioWare Edmonton, even though it seemed like we were just an afterthought.".

But while The Old Republic eventually made back EA's investment the publisher resented the game for failing to meet its lofty expectations at launch.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more.

It has been revealed that "EA hated SWTOR from the beginning," Darrah says, pointing particular blame at then-EA studios boss Patrick Söderlund. "They wanted it really bad, but all indication – and someone from Austin could probably speak to this more than me – it always seemed to me like they wanted it gone pretty much from the instant it released and didn't hit its numbers. They never wanted to invest in it. They always wanted to push it out of the conversation. They talked about pulling people off of it for a really long time. But it did generate money.".

Still, Darrah suggests that the exact same thing happened when BioWare made its next live-service game, Anthem. By that time, MMOs were looking like old news. "Most of them – if you're not WoW – are going to come out, and then they're going to go free-to-play and then they're going to slowly decay away," Darrah says. But he puts EA's perspective like this: "We don't want that. We want Destiny. Destiny's making so much money.".

Then, of course, Anthem came out, had its moment, and slowly decayed away. The irony is that, at this point, The Old Republic – which is still running and receiving fresh content – is set to outlast Anthem, Destiny, and even BioWare itself.

"Maybe most corporations are incapable of learning those lessons," Darrah laments.

Former Dragon Age lead notes EA mismanagement killed BioWare by forcing it into terrible choices: "They made us do something".

It has been revealed that dustin Bailey joined the GamesRadar team as a Staff Writer in May 2022, and is currently based in Missouri. He's been covering games (with occasional dalliances in the worlds of anime and pro wrestling) since 2015, first as a freelancer, then as a news writer at PCGamesN for nearly five years. His love for games was sparked somewhere between Metal Gear Solid 2 and Knights of the Old Republic, and these days you can usually find him splitting his entertainment time between retro gaming, the latest major action-adventure title, or a long haul in American Truck Simulator.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After appearing in both God of War Ragnarok and next year's God of War Laufey, Deborah Ann Woll is about to reprise her role as Faye in Amazon Prime Video's upcoming live-action series.

Variety reports that the God of War cast list is now welcoming a second actor pulled straight from Sony Santa Monica's video game series. Deborah Ann Woll first revealed up in the games as Kratos' wife and Atreus' mother during God of War Ragnarok, but she's also about to enter the spotlight proper in God of War Laufey.

Amazon's God of War cast now includes Dave Bautista (Guardians of the Galaxy) as god killer Kratos, Callum Vinson (Chucky) as Atreus, Mandy Patinkin as Odin and Ólafur Darri Ólafsson as Thor. Alastair Duncan is also making the game-to-show jump by stepping back into the figurative shoes of chatty head Mimir.

In a recent development, earlier in the year, the God of War show halted production when former Kratos actor Ryan Hurst suffered an on-set injury. Bautista soon took over the role and production began again in October - all of Hurst's scenes had to be reshot, of course.

According to recent reports, there's no release date yet for the show, but it's noted to follow the Norse era of the games which began in 2018's more serious and stern revamp. Amazon ordered a two-season run for the show, which apparently means both seasons will be filmed back-to-back.

Meanwhile, God of War Laufey was recently delayed from February 2027 to May 2027, giving the PS5 exclusive slightly more breathing room away from Fable, Persona 4 Revival and Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis.

"We will make the most of each moment until then by putting in the finishing touches and pushing the game to its fullest potential," developer Sony Santa Monica stated at the time. "On behalf of everyone on the team, we appreciate your patience and we'll be back to share more updates soon.".

While the game puts Faye in the leading role as she battles with gods in a multi-mythological afterlife, the studio was quick to note that her journey isn't considered a side game. God of War Laufey will still connect to future games in the series and, yep, Kratos will eventually be back, too.

"Genuinely, I thought I was going to be much more offended by it, but one, I'm not on social media, so that helps, and two, I don't know, I feel totally unbothered," Woll said of the online trolls who were targeting Laufey after its reveal this summer. "Because I just know it's great. It's okay if it's not your cup of tea, but in no universe is it bad.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in today's instance of a sentence I never thought I'd write, English football commentator John Motson has followed in the footsteps of Darth Vader. In the latest instance of a game featuring a dead celebrity's voice reanimated with help from generative AI, EA Sports FC 27 will soon have Motson offering words about passes and shots that clank off the bar despite him having died in 2023.

EA revealed Motson's resurrection for FC 27 to the BBC, with the deceased commentator's voice being made up of combination of old recording sessions and generative AI. The publishers got permission from Motson's widow and son to do this, and told the BBC they'd not have gone ahead if Motson's family - whom EA have paid an undisclosed sum for the rights to use Motson's likeness and recreate his voice - hadn't been on board.

In a recent development, "My dad was the least technological person in the world," Motson's son Fred said. "Till his dying day, he had a typewriter on his desk. So I don't think he would have quite understood what the AI was doing technologically - but I think, on the other hand, he was always really keen to get involved in these kinds of projects.".

According to recent reports, EA senior game design director Mat Prior said AI has been used for the likes of lines in which Motson talks about modern players who don't feature in the old excerpts of him calling games. You'd think that might've been the point at which EA began to question why it's necessary to resurrect Motson for the purpose of commentating on games featuring a number of players he might never have watched while he was alive, meaning we don't know what unique calls he might have made in response to seeing them strut their stuff. Alas, it seems that wasn't the case.

Industry observers note that "From a gaming standpoint, it's something we've used for many years - like machine learning to help drive animation systems and so on and so forth," Prior added. "It's not there to replace commentators in any way shape or form...there's certainly no future looks to replace anyone with AI." It's worth noting EA already use genAI to replicate the voices of some living commentators with their permission, with the justification given being that it helps cut down on the amount of work required to record hours of a real human saying different player names with different inflections.

In a recent development, motson served as a commentator on FIFA 96 through 05, but looks to have been absent from the series since that point aside from briefly popping up for a return in FIFA 19. So, aside from that late 2010s one-off, Motson hadn't been part of one of EA's football games for about two decades prior to this AI-enabled resurrection for FC 27. I'd argue that makes it a lot more difficult to make the case for this use of genAI. It's not like the tech's being used to help maintain continuity with a voice that's always been part of the series' furniture, as is the case with Witcher 3 devs CD Projekt Red's modification of Geralt's Polish voice via genAI in the Songs of the Past DLC following actor Jacek Rozenek's stroke. In that case, the actor was also alive to give his direct permission.

Whether families or estates should be able to permit the use of AI cloning on the voices of actors or performers who didn't give written permission for it while they were alive is a matter of much contention. Actor Peter Caulfield, who's been arguing for greater protections against AI voice cloning through a campaign called Save Our Voices Now, argued in the BBC piece that it should only be allowed in cases where living people have signed deals to allow it.

Sources indicate that personally, I think games should probably do without genAI-fuelled celebrity ressurections, especially in scenarios where there seems no pressing need to do so. Even Tupac's likeness being used without any AI bollocks in RGG Studio's upcoming historical beat 'em up Stranger Than Heaven feels unsettling. AI Motson will be added to FC 27 as an optional commentator on November 26th.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Banjo-Kazooie - the iconic Rare platformer starring an absent-minded bear and the sassy red bird he carries in a backpack - has been on hiatus for years, but a newly introduced Activision job listing has raised hopes for a new game.

In a LinkedIn post advertising a 'Product Manager, Emergent Franchises' role, the publisher wrote that it's "home to iconic gaming franchises including Call of Duty, Crash Bandicoot, Spyro the Dragon, and now… Halo, Age of Empires, Sea of Thieves, and Banjo Kazooie.".

"Become part of the team working on building, growing, and shaping many of these franchises," the listing goes on. "As a Product Manager, you will serve as the publishing product lead for an upcoming premium console & PC title, driving the product from concept to launch.".

According to recent reports, if you're scratching your brain trying to remember when Activision took control of the beloved platformer, well, it happened during Xbox's last massive internal shakeup. Amid the mass layoffs and studio divestments, Xbox also made some drastic changes to its corporate structure - Halo, World's Edge and Rare were all slotted under Activision's supervision.

Rare's 40-year history includes almost too many notable games to list, but the internal rejig presumably put Activision in control of games like Conker, Viva Pinata and Killer Instinct, alongside the aforementioned pirate hit Sea of Thieves and Banjo-Kazooie.

Recent findings suggest that the job post is by no means confirmation that a newly introduced Banjo-Kazooie game is in development, but it is the only series named here that can be considered dormant, perhaps hinting that Activision has intends to revive it down the line. Crash Bandicoot 4 and Spyro: A Realm Beyond lay out a pretty good blueprint for its return, I think.

The last properly latest game in the series came 18 years ago with the Xbox 360's Banjo-Kazooie: Nuts and Bolts, a surprisingly good physics-driven vehicle construction sandbox.

Since then, Banjo and Kazooie demonstrated up as a playable fighter in Super Smash Bros Ultimate. More recently, a fan-made PC port and an Evercade Double Pack have kept the series chugging.

Sources indicate that composer Grant Kirkhope was slightly more hopeful about the prospect of a Banjo-Threeie back in September. "I do know of like three companies that have actually physically pitched to Microsoft or to Rare about making another Banjo-Kazooie game, and I don't think anyone was successful," he mentioned at the time.

  • "Chapte 6 is progressing well," he wrote in a fresh blog post.
  • Sources indicate that while the bones are supposedly all there, Fox explained that he and his team still need to knock out localisation, testing and polishing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Toby Fox has given eager fans an patch on the development of Deltarune Chapter 6 and Chapter 7 - the Undertale follow-up's final two episodes.

"Chapte 6 is progressing well," he wrote in a fresh blog post. "The game is now a structurally complete draft that can be played from the beginning to the end. All the maps, events, and battles exist. (Although there's still one optional event which is dragging out a bit…)".

Sources indicate that while the bones are supposedly all there, Fox explained that he and his team still need to knock out localisation, testing and polishing. "Much of the game looks complete… but, some vital scenes and details are still undercooked in their presentation, so it's going to take a bit longer before we can really move to full-on testing.".

Deltarune Chapter 6 was previously described as a slightly shorter episode that should hopefully set up the game's finale quite nicely. Despite being on the smaller side, Fox mentioned he understandably doesn't want to rush development and "would like it to be as good as possible.".

And since Deltarune's next chapter is almost past the finish line - at least, in some respect - that means certain members of the team have already moved over to Chapter 7.

"Well, we've only just started," Fox continued. "I read out the events and dialogue of Chapter 7 to the team. However, just when the story reached a critical moment, I stopped reading… I told my team they need to complete more of the game before I tell them what happens. Everyone agrees it's more fun this way".

"Unlike every other Chapter, I actually feel like I know what I'm doing this time, so I have a lot of confidence.".

Recent findings suggest that deltarune's been on a long journey to get here, but, thankfully, the end is finally in sight. Deltarune debuted as a free download all the way back in 2018, a second chapter then dropped in 2021, the next two released together four years later, before the arrival of the most recent Chapter 5 this year.

We don't know exactly how long Deltarune's last two chapters might take, but the good news is that it's already been a pretty fantastic game for years. Here's hoping those loose threads don't dangle for much longer.

#167596. Quote of the Day from CEO behind friendslop hits Peak and Content Warning: "Losing is terrible"

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (553 w)

Quote of the Day from CEO behind friendslop hits Peak and Content Warning: "Losing is terrible"

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (553 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gamesradar

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 2026 was a massive year for friendslop, but 2025 was its breakout year.
  • That's according to Petter Henriksson, CEO of Landfall Games, which was one half of Peak alongside Aggro Crab Studios.
  • But that came at something of a cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

2026 was a massive year for friendslop, but 2025 was its breakout year. That's thanks in large part to Peak, which not only drew in millions of players, but helped establish a fresh genre after its developers happily leaned into the new term, despite its less-than-complimentary description. But it was actually 2020 that might have been the most important year for friendslop.

That's according to Petter Henriksson, CEO of Landfall Games, which was one half of Peak alongside Aggro Crab Studios. Speaking about the growth of cooperative games in the latest issue of Edge Magazine, he claims that during the pandemic "gaming became more acceptable as a social endeavour," and that it found mainstream acceptance as "how you create social contact with your friends.".

But that came at something of a cost. During those lockdowns, Henriksson states "we spent a lot of years playing multiplayer together and someone always had to lose." The problem there, he points out, is that "you don't want to play with all your friends in your game and you lose." And that's because, as he so cunningly puts it: "Losing feels terrible.".

Sources indicate that now, before the inevitable joke about why nobody told my League of Legends friends that, I should point out that Henriksson is making a wider point about game design, rather than simply telling you you'd rather win. If the point of playing the game is to spend time with friends, forcing someone to lose isn't necessarily conducive to keeping that group playing. 'Friendslop' maintains stakes, but its generally collaborative approach means that you all win as a team, or all lose as a team - rather than making any one person do better than everyone else.

Henriksson's ideas are hardly new - the idea of friendslop has been pretty mainstream since Among Us was a breakout hit in 2020 - but it's interesting to see this philosophy put forward in such a simple way. Elsewhere in the feature, we hear from the teams behind REPO, Big Walk, and even Wardogs, but it's Henriksson who once again makes an excellent point about how the genre has changed. Peak kicked off a huge swathe of friendly co-op titles, but in doing so it massively raised the bar: "If you make a friendslop game today, it has to be a lot better than it had to be when we did it.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A PC version of Grand Theft Auto 6 - one from unofficial sources, at least - may be closer than we thought. After suddenly returning last week with a near-full build of the Xbox version, notorious leaker CyberLeek has now posted the missing piece they intentionally held back: the game's executable (.exe) file.

Sources indicate that "The exe is out. Always free. An early Christmas gift from CL," CyberLeek reportedly wrote, as relayed on Reddit. "The torch passes to the open source re-comp and emulation projects.".

Hours later, the recompilation modders and hackers part of the Project Leonida Discord server - the current hub for all GTA 6 recompilation efforts - posted footage of the game booting up on PC.

According to recent reports, in just a matter of hours, modders - with the help of Claude AI - managed to turn the leaked Xbox build into a PC port, of sorts. In this Reddit video, you can see the game boot up to the initial setup before hitting a black screen. The build is clearly not yet playable, though Eurogamer has not directly verified those claims.

Shayder, one of the lead developers on Project Leonida, mentioned in a since-deleted post on X that we should "expect a lot of static recompilation work to be done soon." On the project's Discord server, they later clarified that it could take about a week for the build to reach a playable state on PC.

Industry observers note that as for CyberLeek, the leaker is still soliciting donations for a secret project "for the gamers", adding in the build's readme file, "Nobody has to give anything, and every release stays free either way. But every donation is a vote for more of this, and so is every trade of the token.".

Rockstar has not announced a PC version of GTA 6, but the firm has historically released its games on PC several months after their console debut. In October, a report remarked GTA 6's PC version would arrive in the first quarter of 2027, an unusually short gap between the console and PC releases.

These latest recompilation efforts, however, may force Rockstar to speed up development of the PC version. Though the recompiled build may never reach the level of quality or stability of an official port, many of those eager to play the game on PC likely wouldn't care.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Emperor’s New Groove is one of those Walt Disney Animation movies that will forever and always be imprinted in my brain. The 2000 film came out at just the right time in my childhood when I’d put it on repeat. I could honestly quote most of it front to back. However, I had no idea about the experience Kuzco's voice actor, David Spade, had.

The animation movie landscape has changed a lot over the years. These days all the significant roles go to Hollywood names rather than talents known specifically for voice acting. David Spade, who famously got his start on SNL, spoke to this while talking about The Emperor’s New Groove with these words:.

In a recent development, I was the last guy to do a Disney movie where they stated it was ‘an honor’, and that’s why I didn’t get a lot of money. And then, they came out with Shrek, and everyone got $5 million bucks, and I go 'Wait, what the fuck is going on?'.

Industry observers note that hey, he makes a good point. Prior to the 21st Century, animated movies weren't paying significant-name celebrities the big bucks. David Spade was also working with Disney Animation at a time when the studio wasn’t making blockbusters to the degree it is now with the likes of Frozen or Moana. Spade even disclosed how much he made, saying this:.

I got $75,000, which sounds like a lot. It was a lot… They rat fucked me.

Shrek came out in 2001 – one year after The Emperor’s Fresh Groove – and made almost half a billion worldwide. It helped usher in an era of blockbuster animated films led by A-list celebrities that we continue to live in. The Emperor's New Groove made $169 million worldwide, and was actually thought of as a commercial flop at the time of its release.

Spade’s comments about The Emperor’s New Groove were made while on his podcast Fly On The Wall with guest Denis Leary, who famously plays Diego the saber-tooth tiger in the Ice Age movies. Ice Age came out a couple of years after Spade’s Disney movie, and has a sixth installment among upcoming Disney movies in 2027. Leary mentioned he and the rest of the Ice Age cast have received pay bumps since first signing up to the franchise because they are watched so frequently on streaming.

Even though I imagine it’s a bummer that Spade lost out on some cash he might have gotten for the same amount of work a couple of years later on something else, he also made a point of saying he loves The Emperor’s New Groove and how well it turned out. But he did so while pointing out something else about being a voice actor on a Disney film that was hard to deal with in the moment….

In a recent development, no, I did it and it just kept going and going, and I’m like, ‘Guys, I don’t want to drive out to Disney every day and just lay down an hour or two of tracks. I’m like Denis Leary, I have shit to do on my day off. I love the movie now, but during it I was starting to get a little itchy. Like, there’s no ending. I really love it, and they’re miracle workers with the freaking animation.

Sources indicate that animated movies like The Emperor’s Newly introduced Groove famously go through a long production process. The 2000 movie in particular did so because it was actually originally an entirely different movie called Kingdom of the Sun. It was more inspired by The Prince and the Pauper, featured Owen Wilson in a voice role, and Spade was playing a character named Manco instead of Kuzco before they shifted directions. No wonder he was getting antsy while making it!

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

It has been revealed that while I can understand David Spade’s blunt thoughts about working with Disney, I’m so happy he stuck it out and played Kuzco. The movie has brought me so much joy throughout my life, and it’s certainly one of the most beloved projects of his career. You can watch it now with a Disney+ subscription.

Industry observers note that sarah El-Mahmoud has been with CinemaBlend since 2018 after graduating from Cal State Fullerton with a degree in Journalism. In college, she was the Managing Editor of the award-winning college paper, The Daily Titan, where she specialized in writing/editing long-form features, profiles and arts & entertainment coverage, including her first run-in with movie reporting, with a phone interview with Guillermo del Toro for Best Picture winner, The Shape of Water. Now she's into covering YA television and movies, and plenty of horror. Word webslinger. All her writing should be read in Sarah Connor’s Terminator 2 voice over.

Sources indicate that it has been a while since I played Slay the Spire 2. I return to find the forums full of grief concerning a recently introduced sixth character - a minstrel of sorts, dressed in carpets, who shoots arrows out of a harp.

In a recent development, the short version is that the Fool was wildly overpowered when Mega Crit added her to the early access deckbuilder's beta branch, with a base arrow-shooting mechanic that lets her dish out at least 21 damage in her first turn, and a Repeat Shot card that allows for upwards of 80. She ain't so vicious anymore, because they've just released a "mostly Fool-centric" patch that nerfs a couple dozen or so cards.

Recent findings suggest that it's not all nerfs – they've buffed Cho Chorus, Quietus and Show Off, among others, while reworking Tune, Flourescence and Rapid Shot. There's a upcoming Rare card, Optimism, which exhausts all Sadness in your Hand, while drawing a card for every card exhausted.

Sources indicate that some context: Sadness is a special colourless card, earned by way of cards like Mourning Blow. It remains in your hand between turns and can't be played, making it an immediate hindrance, but you can transform it and use it as fuel for certain cards. Just like real sadness! Best of all, you can turn it into Joy, which grants you Energy. Reading about this complex neurophysical alchemy is making me tired. Shall I give the beta build a go? Do I dare to eat a peach? Are you sick of ham-fisted Prufrock references yet?

Read the full patch notes here. The Fool is an interesting creation, eyebrow-raising damage output aside, and I look forward to her addition to the game's main Steam branch. She can play various flavours of music to modify other cards.

I do like a weird bard, and I broadly approve of the practice of releasing fresh early access characters with all the sliders pushed to max, waiting for the cacophonous whining to reach a certain pitch, and then jocularly chopping back their stats. I should get back into Slay the Spire 2. I just have to play [redacted] first.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest report from Windows Central details how Xbox was reportedly looking into removing the paywall that prevents players without Xbox Live from playing online games, only to potentially renege on its decision sometime during production of the next-gen device.
  • "Sources close to Microsoft's looks tell me Xbox Helix was originally conceived as a true console-PC hybrid with access to Windows PC games and stores such as Steam, alongside another major change: no paywall for online multiplayer," says the Windows Central report.
  • Industry observers note that the revised proposal has reportedly been altered thanks to a myriad of factors affecting the Xbox business: new management, rising component costs, and a shifting hardware strategy, are all outlined specifically in the report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest report from Windows Central details how Xbox was reportedly looking into removing the paywall that prevents players without Xbox Live from playing online games, only to potentially renege on its decision sometime during production of the next-gen device.

"Sources close to Microsoft's looks tell me Xbox Helix was originally conceived as a true console-PC hybrid with access to Windows PC games and stores such as Steam, alongside another major change: no paywall for online multiplayer," says the Windows Central report. It goes on to note that this Xbox Live-free proposal was iterated upon under Xbox's previous leadership, but with Asha Sharma's appointment as Xbox head in February, all that apparently changed. I guess she did promise "radically different business models", after all.

Industry observers note that the revised proposal has reportedly been altered thanks to a myriad of factors affecting the Xbox business: new management, rising component costs, and a shifting hardware strategy, are all outlined specifically in the report. We've previously heard that Xbox's next-gen console could cost up to $1,800, with a handheld version coming in 2027 and a full release by holiday 2028 (a Helix console at $1,200 would mean a 50 percent increase on top of Series X's current price, for what it's worth). Sharma has stressed Helix will launch as "a family of devices" that will act as a bridge between PC and Xbox capable of playing games from both platforms.

Sources indicate that if Xbox has, indeed, decided to scrap the idea of free online multiplayer access, it'll be a blow to the idealistic 'PC and Xbox' platform that Microsoft has been touting for the past few years: PC players do not need a subscription in order to access online modes, so - right out the gate - there will be a division between one group of players and the other. Perhaps this is why we've heard a little change in the tone of how Sharma and other Xbox bosses are talking about Helix more recently - these hints that the console will be a true PC-and-console hybrid have died down, and been replaced by insinuations that we'll see more of a traditional console with the "ability to play your PC games.".

Recent findings suggest that xbox has been running Xbox Live as a service since 2002, when it launched on the original Xbox console. By 2005, it was split into gold and silver tiers to distinguish free players from those that paid. In 2023, the service was fully renamed Xbox Game Pass Core, looping in access to the base roster of Game Pass games with online play.
